functionalObligations.text: A depositor sends an ERC-20 (including a liquid staking token) into a whitelisted strategy and receives deposit shares: an internal, non-transferable pro-rata accounting claim, not a token. A Strategy Whitelister, currently the StrategyFactory, controls which strategies are eligible.

[Vl sub-mechanism 1 of 5: validator key registration and vetting] A depositor may instead deploy an EigenPod at a CREATE2 address salted on its own staker address, deposit 32 ETH with the pod as withdrawal credentials, and then prove on chain that a named validator's withdrawal credentials point at that pod; validator state is thereafter maintained by periodic checkpoints.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. This is a credential *proof*, not a registration and not a vetting: nobody approves the validator and nobody may reject it, and the proof binds a beacon-chain object to an execution-layer address. Vl is not used. Note the structural fact this makes visible: EigenPod contains a genuine validator lifecycle while core/ contains a thing that only rhymes with one, and one symbol cannot hold both.

functionalObligations.text: A pod's beacon-chain balance increase raises the owner's deposit shares, while a balance decrease does not lower them and instead reduces a proportional beaconChainSlashingFactor that starts at 1 WAD, so the protocol never carries a share deficit.
functionalObligations.note: Ix is deliberately not used. The scaling factors here (beaconChainSlashingFactor per pod, _depositScalingFactor per staker) are per-position and monotone decreasing by construction; Ix names a *global* index that changes claim value in both directions. Claiming Ix would flatten the asymmetry, which is the whole content of the design.

functionalObligations.text: A staker delegates its entire position to an operator; the delegation transfers no custody, no assets and no transaction authority, only the right to be counted as that operator's weight and the corresponding slashing liability.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Au is the nearest symbol and is deliberately not used: Au is delegated *execution* scope and law L17 asks it for bounded scope, revocation, expiry and nonce/domain separation. delegateTo moves no assets and grants no call rights; what is delegated is liability. The staker-to-operator-to-AVS graph is EigenLayer's core object and the vocabulary has no edge for it.

functionalObligations.text: An operator registers by naming a delegation approver, whose signature it may then require before any staker may delegate to it, and an allocation delay of its own choosing.
functionalObligations.note: Aw names the approver gate. It does not name the fact that operator identity lives in one contract (DelegationManager) and per-set membership in another (AllocationManager), so that 'being an operator' is two separate registrations with different admission rules.

functionalObligations.text: [Vl sub-mechanism 2 of 5: stake allocation and scheduling] An operator allocates a magnitude, a proportion of its delegated stake in a given strategy, to a named operator set; allocations are held per (operator, strategy, operator set) with a current magnitude, a pending diff and an effect block, and deallocations are processed through a per-(operator, strategy) queue in order.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE, and structurally different from Lido's scheduler (which allocates *principal* to operators). Here what is allocated is *slashability* over principal that does not move. The vocabulary has neither object. Bs names the capital; it does not name a budget over the capital's exposure.

functionalObligations.text: [Whether the same collateral can be committed twice] The sum of an operator's allocated magnitudes across all operator sets can never exceed INITIAL_TOTAL_MAGNITUDE (1e18, one WAD), which is reduced only by slashing, so the same *deposit* backs many operator sets but each unit of *slashability* is exclusively allocated and no two operator sets can slash the same stake.
functionalObligations.note: CORRECTION, and the load-bearing one for this application. The corpus residue entry asserts that in EigenLayer 'the same collateral is simultaneously bonded to mutually-unaware slashing laws'. Unique Stake exists precisely to prevent that, and it is enforced by arithmetic rather than by convention: 'The sum of all magnitude allocations never being greater than the Total Magnitude ensures the property of Unique Stake... ensures that no two Operator Sets can slash the same stake.' Stage 2 does not carry the old framing. What remains RESIDUE is the object itself: nothing in the 58 names a conserved, partitionable slashability budget, monotone decreasing and reduced only by loss.

functionalObligations.text: [What the restaked collateral secures] The allocated stake secures an arbitrary external service, an AVS, whose duties, faults and correctness conditions the core protocol does not model and cannot read.
functionalObligations.note: Rs is a CANDIDATE and is used with the mark. It is exact in name and thin in content: it asserts that restaking is present and stops. Law L22 asks Rs for an attributed slash condition, non-reflexive capital and a loss waterfall; the first is present (F9), the second holds for LST and native ETH strategies, and the third is F11 and F12.

functionalObligations.text: [Who may write a slashing condition] Any AVS may create an operator set, define its slashable strategies and its membership roster, and call slashOperator with a proportion in WAD; the core protocol validates the arithmetic and never the ground for the slash. ELIP-006 states the consequence plainly: an attacker who gains access to AVS keys can drain the entirety of operator and staker allocated stake.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Aw is retained in the construction for F1 and F5 but is not claimed here: Aw carries the gate and drops the law. The significant part is not that an AVS controls admission to its set, it is that an AVS authors the predicate under which other people's capital is destroyed, and the protocol that holds the capital cannot express what the predicate says.

functionalObligations.text: AVSDirectory is deprecated and AllocationManager is the sole registration path from an AVS to an operator set.
functionalObligations.note: Recorded because any decomposition anchored on AVSDirectory is stale. The published docs index still stamps itself EigenLayer v1.3.0 while the latest release is v1.13.0; the per-contract docs under docs/core/ are current and the index is not.

functionalObligations.text: [Vl sub-mechanism 5 of 5: penalty attribution] A slash reduces the operator's currentMagnitude, maxMagnitude and encumberedMagnitude proportionally and processes pending deallocations pro rata, so the loss falls on every staker delegated to that operator in that strategy and on no one else.
functionalObligations.note: Sl is used and is a better fit here than in Lido: the loss is socialised across a *named* claim class, the delegators of one operator in one strategy, rather than across the whole supply. Bs is used because the allocated stake is genuinely slashable first-loss capital rented out, which is the closest fit any symbol achieves anywhere in this category. What Sl cannot express is that the size of the class is itself a variable the operator controls through F6.

functionalObligations.text: Slashed shares are first marked burnable-or-redistributable, and only after SLASH_RESOLUTION_DELAY_BLOCKS may anyone permissionlessly clear them, sending them either to the burn address 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000E16E4 or to the operator set's redistribution recipient.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE on two counts, and NEW: the resolution delay shipped in release v1.13.0 on 2026-06-25, after the corpus record. First, a loss that has been *recorded* but not yet *effected*, awaiting a permissionless poke after a delay, is a state nothing in the vocabulary marks. Second, Sl assigns a loss to a claim class; ELIP-006 assigns it to a named counterparty as restitution, at an address fixed immutably at operator-set creation so stakers can price the risk at opt-in. That is a remedy, not an allocation, and the vocabulary cannot express the difference.

functionalObligations.text: Native ETH and EIGEN are excluded from redistribution: native ETH because paying a recipient would require beacon exits whose queue can range from hours to weeks, and EIGEN because it requires a delay on token protocol outflow for its intersubjective machinery.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. The corpus records redistribution as prospective and records neither that it is live on mainnet nor the exclusions, and the exclusions are the interesting part: the protocol's own two native assets are the two that cannot be redistributed. Nothing names an asset-conditional loss remedy.

functionalObligations.text: [Vl sub-mechanism 4 of 5: exit] A staker undelegates or queues a withdrawal, waits MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY_BLOCKS (100,800 blocks on mainnet, about 14 days), and then completes the queued withdrawal either as shares or as tokens; for native ETH the beacon-chain exit queue sits underneath and is not modelled by these contracts.
functionalObligations.note: Wq names the staker's queue and Ep the block-height gate. The validator-side exit that must complete underneath it for native restakers is outside the contract set entirely, which is the same gap Lido has, arrived at by a different route: Lido models the validator exit and does not name it, EigenLayer does not model it at all.

functionalObligations.text: Five further delays bind, each for a different party's benefit: ALLOCATION_CONFIGURATION_DELAY of 126,000 blocks (17.5 days) before a new allocation binds, so stakers can leave before new risk attaches; an operator-chosen allocation delay; DEALLOCATION_DELAY of 100,800 blocks after which deregistration ends exposure, so an AVS keeps recourse; the withdrawal delay of F14; and the slash resolution delay of F12.
functionalObligations.note: Ep names a gated transition and is retained. RESIDUE recorded here: Ep names an epoch and Wq a queue, and neither names a delay whose purpose is to give a *third party* time to react. Deregistering from an operator set does not end exposure, which is the clearest case: the delay exists solely so that the counterparty retains recourse against someone who has already left. The corpus lists this as one security parameter; it is now five.

functionalObligations.text: An AVS funds a rewards submission weighted across strategies, or an operator-directed submission scoped to an operator set for operators registered during the period; a singleton rewardsUpdater posts distribution roots that become claimable after an activation delay, and earners claim against Merkle proofs or nominate a claimer. The operator's default split is 1000 basis points, a flat 10%.
functionalObligations.note: Fd is a CANDIDATE symbol, used with the required mark. CORRECTION: Em is DROPPED and Fd is ADDED. Em names protocol-funded emissions; these rewards are funded by the AVS that submits them, and reach earners as a distribution of received value. The corpus carries Em with no supporting marker. UNKNOWN and flagged: EmissionsController.sol exists in src/contracts/core/ with no coverage in docs/ at the commit stage 1 read, together with ProtocolRegistry.sol and ReleaseManager.sol; if EmissionsController is what its name suggests, Em may become load-bearing and should be re-tested rather than inherited. CALCULATION_INTERVAL_SECONDS and MAX_REWARDS_DURATION are named without values.

functionalObligations.text: An AVS registers an operator-table calculator and a global configuration per operator set on the source chain; on a destination chain, an updater accepts a signed GlobalTableRoot and verifies individual operator tables against it by Merkle proof, with an EigenLabs-operated Generator calculating and signing the root and a permissionless Transporter distributing it.
functionalObligations.note: ADDED. Xm names the verification and law L18 asks it for explicit finality, chain binding and replay protection. RESIDUE recorded here: what is being transported is not a message about an asset but *the security state itself*, exported to a domain where it will be relied upon, with a single named off-chain signer at the root of it. Nothing distinguishes exporting a stake table from delivering a message.

functionalObligations.text: For faults that are obvious to human observers but not provable in the EVM, the designed fallback is forking the EIGEN token: a challenger creates a fork in which the malicious stakers are slashed, and AVSs and users choose which fork to respect.
functionalObligations.note: RESIDUE. Oa is the nearest symbol and is deliberately not used: Oa is an on-chain dispute game with a bonded challenger and a verifier, and a social fork of a token has neither, its outcome being which asset the market prices. UNCONFIRMED at primary source: docs.eigencloud.xyz blocked automated fetch (403) and blog.eigencloud.xyz presented a TLS certificate mismatch, so the design is sourced through search summaries. UNKNOWN whether intersubjective slashing is implemented on mainnet.

functionalObligations.text: A dedicated pause flag can halt the burn-and-redistribution flow independently of the rest of the protocol.
functionalObligations.note: Shipped with v1.13.0. A pause scoped to one flow rather than to a contract is finer than Gp expresses, but the symbol discharges the obligation.

functionalObligations.text: The core contracts are upgradeable and a permissions controller mediates who may act for whom.
functionalObligations.note: CORRECTION: Tg is DROPPED. Stage 1 found no first-party citation of a governance timelock for EigenLayer, and invariant 5 of the run is cite-or-drop. Law L15 (Up requires Tg or a bounded emergency process) is therefore UNMET on the available evidence; F19's pause is the only bounded emergency process cited. UNKNOWN whether a timelock exists: this is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence, and stage 3 should record it as such rather than as a defect. Stage 1 also did not verify deployed implementation addresses against the v1.13.0 tag, so deployed-to-repo correspondence is UNKNOWN. Licence note for the paper rather than the checker: the reference implementation is BUSL-1.1 (Layr Labs, Inc.) with change dates 2025-05-01 and 2027-02-06 to MIT and a production-use restriction.

functionalObligations.text: [Vl sub-mechanism 3 of 5: deposit front-running defence] There is none, and none is needed: the pod is deployed at an address deterministic in the staker's own address, and the same party that supplies the 32 ETH also owns the withdrawal credentials it is deposited against, so the adversary Lido's DepositSecurityModule exists to defeat, an operator capturing a pool's ETH by pre-registering the pubkey against different credentials, has no counterpart here.
functionalObligations.note: Not residue: the obligation is closed by construction because depositor and credential owner are the same party. The empty array records this identically to an unnamed mechanism, which it is not, and that conflation is the formalism finding this stage keeps reproducing across lanes. Three of Vl's five sub-mechanisms are present here (F2, F6, F14) plus penalty attribution (F11); this one does not arise, and stake allocation (F6) is present in a form that allocates exposure rather than principal.
